blocks.text: The Syriac ܐܦܪܫ, in the Aphel conjugation, agrees: he pricked.

"The meaning: it exhales poison, which is commonly attributed to the basilisk and is not to be counted among fables. For certain kinds of serpents at some times exhale something intoxicating and inducing sleep, by which they also catch animals. See by all means my son, Christian Friedrich Michaelis, who has described this from his own experience, in the Goettingisches Magazin, vierten Iahrgang erstes Stück, no. 5, über die Klapperschlange, p. 106 ff. This will indeed be said excellently and with such knowledge of nature that I seem to myself to prefer it; at any rate I would think the first place should be assigned to this explanation." So J. D. Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 6, p. 2043. I prefer Bochart's interpretation, since the parallelism of the members commends it, as Bochart himself will point out shortly.

Or because they thought it was said of flying, from spreading the wings, as among the Arabs تفرّش [tafarrasha] means a bird released into the air hovered in the same place with its wings spread and moving.

Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 1, p. 52, renders מאורות as luminaries, a name by which he thinks the Hebrews called the feelers, or horns of the cerastes, which serve it as luminaries for tracking its prey. That eminent man would, I think, have refrained from this interpretation had this note of Bochart's been known to him.

The ملكة [malika] of the Arabs and the βασιλισκος [basiliskos] of the Greeks seem to be the same species of serpent that Laurenti, in the Amphibia, p. 87, no. 189, calls Coronella petola, and Linnaeus, in the Syst. vol. 1, part 3, p. 1112, Pethola. Since this species has several varieties, I would refer to the Arabs' ملكة [malika] the coronella cerastoides, subfuscescens [III, 192] maculis dilute fuscescentibus, in Laurenti, p. 86, no. 185. Common to this whole species is a head covered in the middle of the forehead, between the eyes, with a shining shield like a crown, whence the names coronella, βασιλίσκος [basiliskos] and ملكة [malika], regulus, were given to it.
